content: The program was financially supported by the National Office for Nutrition (ONN) and supplemented by the Global Fund. To expand the intervention, the National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) identified over 120 facilities in regions with a high prevalence of tuberculosis (TB) and significant levels of undernutrition among TB patients. Insights from the World Food Programme (WFP) nutrition initiative guided the NTP in establishing a standardized national protocol for assessing and managing the nutritional needs of individuals with TB. To facilitate nutritional status assessments, WFP provided anthropometric equipment to all TB diagnostic and treatment centers. Additionally, WFP coordinated the distribution of specialized nutritious foods to TB facilities, ensuring regular deliveries every two months to maintain adequate stock levels. To monitor the necessity and impact of nutritional support for TB patients, the NTP incorporated nutrition-related indicators into its data collection tools. In 2021, WFP conducted an evaluation of the nutritional support program, which revealed a 90% recovery rate among recipients of the intervention. The collaboration between NTP, WFP, and ONN successfully scaled up efforts to address malnutrition among TB patients in southern Madagascar. WFP’s logistical support enabled comprehensive assessments of the nutritional status of TB patients and ensured a reliable supply of specialized nutritious foods. The implementation and scaling of the intervention were phased based on assessments of the combined burden of TB, malnutrition, and food insecurity. The development of a standardized protocol for nutritional assessment and support facilitated the routine implementation of the intervention. Routine monitoring and evaluation, including standardized indicators, have been instrumental in tracking the combined burden and effectiveness of the response. Efforts also extended to supporting individuals with TB and comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, people who use drugs, and those living with HIV), as well as their families and communities, in areas such as healthcare delivery (including peer support initiatives), quality of care assessments, advocacy for improved service coverage, stigma reduction, and health literacy initiatives. Social protection measures, such as nutritional support, employment guarantees, safe housing, and poverty alleviation, were promoted to mitigate the financial burden of TB and its comorbidities. Advocacy for health insurance coverage aimed to reduce out-of-pocket expenses and ensure access to essential services not freely available in public healthcare systems. Digital technologies, including telemedicine, video-supported treatment, computer-aided TB detection on chest radiography, and digital data collection tools, were recommended to enhance service delivery. Countries were encouraged to adopt and adapt these technologies for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, ensuring interoperability between TB and comorbidity information systems while safeguarding patient privacy. Plans for the long-term sustainability of digital tools, including software updates and equipment maintenance, were emphasized. Phased scaling of people-centered services for TB and comorbidities was recommended, starting with screening and gradually expanding to prevention and co-management within the same facilities. For example, in countries with strong TB service networks but less established diabetes services, initial efforts could focus on diabetes screening and co-management among TB patients. Services addressing multimorbidity, such as mental health conditions, diabetes, and malnutrition, were also suggested within TB/HIV service models. India’s collaborative TB/HIV activities serve as a model for other countries. These activities were strategically scaled from high-burden states to nationwide coverage, supported by a national TB/HIV framework, coordination mechanisms, joint training modules, and surveillance systems. Intensified TB/HIV packages included HIV testing for all TB patients, referrals for antiretroviral therapy (ART), and strengthened infection prevention measures. By 2020, the proportion of TB patients with HIV test results increased from 11% to 92%, and 1 million people with HIV received TB preventive treatment. Operational and implementation research were highlighted as critical for informing policy, programming, and service delivery. Clear definitions of indicators and regular monitoring facilitated progress and accountability. WHO guidelines provided standardized approaches for monitoring TB and comorbidities, with data from various sectors (e.g., prisons, mining, social services) supporting multisectoral action. The rapid development of digital technology offers opportunities for data collection and analysis. Interoperable electronic systems, such as DHIS2, can support co-management, referrals, and real-time epidemiological analysis while ensuring patient confidentiality. Recording and reporting tools should be updated to capture data on the continuum of care for TB and comorbidities. Countries were encouraged to harmonize systems, train staff, and establish mechanisms for data collection across sectors. Finally, embedding indicators for TB and comorbidities into routine systems, building capacity at all levels, and conducting systematic data reviews were recommended to strengthen monitoring and evaluation. Disseminating results to healthcare workers through supervision and mentoring was suggested to incentivize continued implementation and improvement.
